I need to research Prop 41 before deciding whether to vote yes or no.

Prop 41 mandates audits of programs funded by new special taxes and bars any new state tax from being exempted from the Gann spending limit.

Prop 41 would nullify any conflicting measure if it passes. I need to weigh the Gann limit's impact, the billionaire tax's merits, and whether the audit provisions are independently sound.

I am reviewing independent editorial endorsements and the Legislative Analyst's analysis. The arguments for voting yes include transparency through audits, ensuring new taxes respect the Gann spending limit so excess revenues are refunded, and the fact that this measure does not raise taxes.

Arguments against Prop 41 include its role as a poison pill targeting the billionaire tax. The measure was funded by billionaires including Sergey Brin. Its title emphasizes audits, but the Gann limit prohibition is the operative mechanism that would nullify Prop 40. It could also threaten existing taxes such as MCO fees and hospital quality assurance fees.

The Gann limit is widely viewed as a dysfunctional 1979 constraint that forces refunds or cuts when revenues rise. Most successful recent tax measures exempt themselves from it for good reason.

The audit requirements are slanted. They mandate 10% cuts and compare to the private sector, burdening every special tax initiative regardless of whether it qualifies.

A constitutional amendment is difficult to undo. The single-subject issue could lock California into 1979 fiscal rules. The measure is poorly drafted with reckless collateral damage.

The better vote is no. The measure was designed primarily to obstruct the billionaire tax rather than serve good government.

The Gann limit caps appropriations based on 1978-79 spending adjusted for population and inflation. Excess revenues must be split between taxpayer rebates and education, while other spending gets squeezed.

Voters and the legislature have repeatedly exempted dedicated taxes from the Gann limit. Applying that limit to dedicated revenues would trigger rebates of money voters intended for specific purposes or crowd out other essential spending. Prop 41 would permanently ban any new tax from using these well-established, voter-approved mechanisms. That is not neutral protection of a spending limit. It would make it nearly impossible to fund new dedicated programs without cutting existing ones.

Legal scholars have identified concrete litigation risks to core healthcare financing mechanisms. These include the Prop 35 MCO tax, which lifts the Gann limit for four years and draws billions in federal matching funds. They also cover the Hospital Quality Assurance Fee, skilled nursing facility fees, the Prop 3 millionaire tax extension for education, and the SB 125 Medi-Cal Stability Fund. These are not fringe concerns but fundamental funding structures.

Even if courts ultimately reject the challenges, the litigation risk and "inoperative if enjoined" clauses in hospital fee statutes create real danger.

The audit provisions are poorly designed. They trigger at 25% of signatures before qualification. The General Fund would pay for these audits if the measure fails or does not qualify. This creates a tool to force expensive audits by merely starting signature gathering.

The audit requirements are constitutionally rigid and difficult to adjust. Ongoing audits paid from special tax revenues would also drain money away from the programs voters funded.

The conflict clause would nullify any measure with different audit rules entirely, not merely modify it. That could wipe out Prop 3's existing audit provisions.

Editorial consensus appears to be no. The San Francisco Chronicle called Prop 41 a cynical poison pill. The Santa Cruz Sentinel recommends rejecting Prop 41 and 42 because they tie the state's hands far into the future.

Prop 42 is the more direct vehicle for blocking wealth taxes.

Voting yes on Prop 41 would permanently lock in its Gann restrictions even if Prop 40 fails on its own. The case against the measure is strong regardless of one's position on the billionaire tax.

The only people who should vote yes are those who want to permanently restrict dedicated taxes outside the Gann limit and accept slanted audits in exchange for collateral damage to existing health financing.

I am checking whether a strong case for yes exists that I have undervalued. The Hoover Institution frames the measure as restoring budget discipline because California spending has grown rapidly.

The argument for yes is weaker than it first appeared. The Legislative Analyst's Office states the fiscal effect is unknown and does not claim savings. The 79 percent spending increase since 2019 includes pandemic surges, inflation, and population growth rather than pure policy drift. The Gann limit already exists; the real issue is whether new dedicated taxes can be exempted from it.

Endorsement: Prop 41 is a cynical poison pill. And it isn’t the only one on California’s ballot
Prop 41 is one of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
It wouldn’t be a California election without a few petty, revenge-motivated ballot measures.
Proposition 41 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop41-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is one of two poison pill attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax. The measure explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 41 or its cousin initiative Prop 42 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-proposition-42-taxes-22449389.php) pass with a larger number of votes.
Backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php), Prop 41 would require new special taxes that raise money for specific purposes to adhere to state spending rules, while mandating regular audits of the programs they fund.
What’s so bad about ensuring California spends tax revenue wisely?

Well, nothing — if that’s what the measure actually does. But it’s a cheap ruse to nullify Prop 40.
The measure targets an obscure — but extremely consequential — spending rule embedded in California’s Constitution.
Known as the Gann Limit (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4416), that rule prevents the state from spending more money per taxpayer than it did in 1979 — the year voters approved the measure — once adjusted for inflation. Any money the state collects over the limit must be either refunded to taxpayers or spent on certain purposes, such as infrastructure or education.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 41 would prohibit any state tax taking effect on or after Jan. 1, 2026 from sidestepping those requirements. That would neuter Prop 40, which explicitly exempts its one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires from the Gann Limit to backfill federal healthcare cuts.
Loren Kaye, former president of a California Chamber of Commerce-affiliated think tank and a Prop 41 supporter, told us in an endorsement interview that the measure establishes a “level playing field so that everybody is similarly affected once you reach the limit.”
We agree that budget carveouts generally aren’t a good idea. But the Gann Limit isn’t sacrosanct; there are perfectly legitimate reasons for excluding certain revenues from its rules.
Consider California’s Hospital Quality Assurance Fee Program (https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/providers-partners/hospital-quality-assurance-fee-program-hqaf/), which charges hospitals a fee to unlock matching federal healthcare funds and improve services for low-income patients. These funds are currently exempt from the Gann Limit (https://funds.dof.ca.gov/app/download/3158) — a provision voters approved when they green-lighted Prop 52 in 2016 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=52&year=2016).
But the federal government, which has to approve the tax, could easily demand changes to its structure. If that were to happen and Prop 41 passes, the hospital fee program could arguably be considered a “new” special tax — and thus be subject to the Gann Limit, diverting money away from hospitals, argued David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and Prop 41 opponent.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
California’s financial regulations are impossibly complex after decades of ballot-box budgeting. Adding another restriction is only bound to make things worse.
Meanwhile, Prop 41’s audit requirements are, as Darien Shanske, a UC Davis School of Law professor and Prop 41 opponent, put it, meant to be “the chocolate coating that’s supposed to attract people.”
But they’re largely redundant and would decrease efficiency.
Prop 41 requires the state auditor to evaluate programs that will receive funding from new citizen-proposed special taxes and include its findings in the official voter information guide. But the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office already assesses each ballot initiative’s fiscal and practical impact (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop41-110326.pdf) — including at the 25% signature-gathering threshold Prop 41 identifies — and those analyses are included in the voter guide.
The measure’s ongoing audit requirement could also be counterproductive; tax measures typically contain accountability provisions, and adding an untold number of audits to the already overworked auditor’s office could distract from other critical investigations. Furthermore, Prop 41 directs the state auditor’s office to find 10% annual savings in program costs, which is arbitrary and dilutes the office’s independence.

I have a solid picture of the proposition. I will now check SPUR's full recommendation, the LAO Gann limit background, and Newsom's position on 41.

Most editorial boards and independent experts recommend voting NO. The Chronicle, McClatchy papers, Mercury News, East Bay Times, SPUR, and Santa Cruz Sentinel all oppose the proposition. Only the Southern California News Group supports it. The weight of independent analysis favors rejecting 41.

The audit framing is a ruse. The Gann limit lock-in would harm healthcare financing. The proposition was drafted to nullify Prop 40 via a conflict clause, funded by billionaires. Even opponents of the wealth tax say this goes too far. The evidence-based conclusion is that voting no is better public policy.

Prop 41 is a poor instrument even for those who oppose the wealth tax. Prop 42 would be a more targeted block. Voting no on 40 alone could stop the tax if it fails. If 40 passes with more votes than 41, 41 becomes void entirely including its audit provisions. A yes vote on 41 only works as a poison pill if it outpolls 40.

The permanent constitutional restriction is the harmful part that survives if Prop 40 fails and Prop 41 passes. I will answer no.

Section 3 of Prop 41 prohibits exemptions from the state spending limit for all state taxes, not merely special taxes. This makes the Gann limit restriction far broader than initially apparent.

The definition of exempted tax is extremely broad. It covers revenues deposited outside the General Fund and appropriations increased by statutory Section 4 of Article XIII B. This would block many existing mechanisms.

Article XIII B Section 4 allows the appropriations limit to be established or changed by electors, not merely by statute. This means the broad exemption definition in Prop 41 would block voter-approved increases to the spending limit.

Prop 35 used Section 4 to lift the spending ceiling. If its MCO tax takes effect in 2027, Prop 41 would bar collection. Subparagraph (b) also bars the state from collecting any tax that is exempted.

Prop 41 would ban the entire tax if its structure exempts it from the Gann limit. It does not merely void the exemption and count the revenue toward the limit. This makes it a nuclear option that would nullify Prop 40 rather than merely subjecting its revenues to the spending cap.

Prop
41
CA
Prop
41
|
Constitutional Amendment
Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues From State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes.
Requires audits of citizen initiatives for special taxes. Imposes spending limits on all new special taxes.
SPUR's Recommendation
More transparency and accountability in government spending are worthy objectives. However, the Legislative Analyst’s Office and the state auditor already have the authority to evaluate policies and programs to ensure they are equitable and efficient. Prop. 41 was primarily placed on the ballot to defeat Prop. 40, a measure to tax billionaires. In addition, it would constrain local and state governments’ ability to raise revenue now and in the future for much-needed housing, transportation, infrastructure, and social services, which are already facing cuts at the federal and state levels.
Vote NO
What Prop. 41 Would Do
Proposition 41 would require the state auditor, working with the Legislative Analyst’s Office, to conduct an independent review of any state-level citizen initiative that aims to create a new special tax once it reaches 25% of the required signature threshold to be placed on the ballot. (Special taxes differ from general taxes in that they dedicate revenue to a specific purpose.) All new state-level special taxes would be audited every four years.
Additionally, any new special taxes passed after January 1, 2026 — whether proposed through legislation or through voter initiatives — would be subject to the Gann Limit, a voter-imposed revenue spending limit explained in the Backstory section below.
The audit of proposed citizen initiatives would examine the individual programs that would receive funding through the special tax and assess whether the programs are sufficiently cost-efficient in their hiring and operating practices. It would recommend how the programs could save 10% of their costs. The audit information would be included in the voter information guide, which would increase printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per initiative, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
If a special tax passes, the state auditor would be required to conduct audits every four years to assess spending, evaluate efficiency, and recommend improvements. The auditor would consider public input when measuring the program’s effectiveness. The revenues generated would cover implementation costs. However, the state would pay the initial audit cost if voters rejected the special tax.
Prop. 41 is a countermeasure to the so-called billionaire tax, Prop. 40 (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/ca-prop-40-billionaire-tax). If both measures pass, the one receiving more votes would prevail.
The Backstory
Special taxes are taxes whose revenues are dedicated to a specific purpose rather than contributing to the state’s general fund budget. The State Legislature can levy special taxes with two-thirds voter approval, or an initiative placed on the ballot by voter signatures can do so with a simple majority (50% plus one vote). Currently, special taxes have no audit requirements or spending caps.
Since the late 1970s, California has faced numerous tax limitations through Prop. 13 and other constitutional amendments. The Gann Limit imposes requirements on how the state can spend General Fund revenues. If the state’s revenues exceed the Gann Limit — a dollar amount based on the state’s spending level in 1978–1979, adjusted for population and per capita income — half of revenues over the limit must be allocated to K–14 education and the other half returned to taxpayers. 1 Historically, the Gann Limit has rarely affected distribution of the state’s revenues, but if the state experiences strong income gains (including business/corporate/stock gains) over the limit, it could result in decreasing investment in state priorities such as housing, health care, economic development, and infrastructure.
The fiscal impacts of Prop. 41 are unknown. Adding pages to the voter information guide would cost money, but the audits could also create savings. If this measure prevents the state from raising new revenues from future taxes, it could have a significant negative fiscal impact in the longer term.
Prop. 41 is a countermeasure to Prop. 40, a one-time special tax on individuals with more than $1 billion in assets. Prop. 40 is intended to offset federal funding cuts to critical social safety net programs, including Medi-Cal, CalFresh, and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. The revenues generated from Prop. 40 would be exempt from the Gann Limit.
Prop. 41 was placed on the ballot through a signature-gathering effort led by Building a Better California, which is funded by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other billionaires. It requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass. If it passes with more votes than Prop. 40, it would nullify Prop. 40. (Building a Better California has also placed Prop. 42 (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/ca-prop-42-personal-property-taxes), a separate countermeasure to Prop. 40, on the ballot.)
Equity Impacts
Restricting spending from special taxes could negatively affect efforts to fund health care, food assistance, and other programs that disproportionately benefit lower-income Californians and communities of color.
Pro
Audits of proposed citizen initiatives could help ensure that the programs they would fund are cost-effective.
Cons
Prop. 41 was placed on the ballot to prevent a competing measure from succeeding. It could affect the state’s ability to raise revenue from other tax measures in the future.
Applying spending limits to new revenue measures could constrain local and state governments’ ability to fund urgent priorities amid unprecedented federal and state budget cuts.
Vote NO

April 21, 2021
The State Appropriations Limit
Introduction
How the Limit Works for the State
How the Limits Work for Other Entities
Why Is the SAL a Constraint for the State Now?
How Might the SAL Limit State Spending Growth?
Administrative Issues in the SAL
How Can the Legislature Respond?
Constructing a Plan
Executive Summary
The State Appropriations Limit (SAL) Likely to Limit Spending Growth in the Budget Year and Future Years
SAL Will Be an Important Issue at May Revision. Proposition 4 (197 9) e stablished an appropriations limit on the state and most types of local governments. The appropriations limit is based on appropriations from tax revenue. If the state has revenues above the limit over two consecutive years, the State Constitution requires the state to split the excess between taxpayer rebates and additional spending on schools. In the Governor's budget, the administration estimated the state would have revenues in excess of the limit in some years between 2018‑19 and 2021‑22. Specifically, according to initial estimates, the state has excess revenues of about $ 100 m illion between 2018‑19 and 2019‑20 and about $ 500 m illion between 2019‑20 and 2020‑21. These amounts represent less than 1 p ercent of the limit in these years. The administration will update its estimates at the May Revision. In light of strong revenue collections that have occurred since January, we anticipate responding to the requirements of the SAL will be an important issue for the state budget this year.
SAL Likely to Be a Major Issue Over the Next Few Years. Our analysis suggests the SAL will be an even more important factor in the state budget in the coming years. The figure below shows our projections of the likely "room" under the limit over the next few years. Projections of the amount of room under the limit are highly uncertain, as shown by the wide range of possible outcomes in the figure. That said, under the vast majority of likely outcomes, we anticipate the state will have "negative room." That is, the state either would need to reduce taxes or issue refunds to taxpayers and make additional payments to schools in these amounts. Further, without significant budget changes, the state likely does not have the capacity for new services or program expansions.
Why Is the Limit an Issue Now?
There are two primary reasons that room under the limit has diminished. First, growth in personal income tax revenue-the state's largest revenue source-has exceeded the SAL's growth rate. There are a few reasons for this, but two important factors are: ( 1) t he state's tax rate structure combined with ( 2) f aster income growth among high‑income earners. As a result, year‑to‑year growth in appropriations has been higher than increases in the SAL. Second, constitutionally required school spending-driven by faster state revenue growth-has increased faster than school limits. Because the state absorbs appropriations above school limits, this trend has resulted in diminished room for the state.
How Can the Legislature Respond?
Options for Legislative Consideration. In the coming months and years, the Legislature will face decisions about how to respond to state tax revenues nearing the limit. This report describes various options that the Legislature could consider in response. They fall into five categories: ( 1) i ssue tax refunds and allocate excess revenues to schools, ( 2) i ncrease spending on excluded purposes, ( 3) r educe proceeds of taxes and spending, ( 4) m ake statutory changes to the SAL, and ( 5) g o to the voters.
Short‑ and Long‑Term Options Needed. Few of these options, in isolation, are likely to be sufficient to keep the state from exceeding the limit over the next few years. For example, this year, the Legislature could decide to issue refunds and provide additional funding to schools. This response might not be sustainable over the long term, however. As existing program costs increase, revenues available for appropriation could be insufficient to meet current service levels. Consequently, changes to the state's revenues and expenditures would be required. Alternatively, should the Legislature pursue statutory changes to the SAL, those changes would be unlikely to be sufficient to avoid reaching the limit in the next few years. In that case, considering placing a measure before the voters could be needed.
Constructing a Plan. We recommend the Legislature construct a short‑ and long‑term plan for how it wishes to respond. To aid the Legislature in constructing this plan, the figure below summarizes the options presented in this report, when each option could take effect, and our estimate of the potential magnitude of each potential change.

Introduction
In the late 1970s, voters passed Proposition 4 (1979), which added Article XIIIB to the State Constitution. Article XIIIB established an appropriations limit on the state and most types of local governments. (These limits also are referred to as "Gann limits" in reference to one of the measure's coauthors, Paul Gann.) The appropriations limits later were amended by Proposition 111, which was passed by voters in 1990. The purpose of the appropriations limits is to keep real (inflation adjusted) per‑person government spending under 1978‑ 79 l evels. For more information about the history of the appropriations limit, see our previous reports, including The 2017‑18 Budget: Governor's Gann Limit Proposal (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2017/3596/gann-limit-030217.pdf), The State Appropriations Limit (https://lao.ca.gov/2000/041300_gann/041300_gann.html), and An Analysis of Proposition 4 t he Gann "Spirit of 13" Initiative (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/1979/20_analysis_of_proposition_4_the_gann_spirit_of_13_initiative.pdf).
At the time of Governor's budget this year, the Department of Finance (DOF) expects the state to collect revenues in excess of the limit in some years between 2018‑19 and 2021‑22. The administration will update this estimate at the May Revision. As such, the state appropriations limit (SAL) or "the limit" will be an important issue in state budgeting this spring. Perhaps more importantly, as discussed in this report, our estimates suggest the growth in state appropriations subject to the limit are likely to significantly outpace growth in the limit in the coming years. Absent a revenue downturn in the coming years, the Legislature most likely will have to make major changes to state budgeting.
This report begins with background information on how the limit works for the state, school districts, and local governments. Next, we explain why the limit is a constraint for state government. Importantly, our analysis suggests this constraint will be a major issue for California in the next few years. Then we discuss some administrative issues in the appropriations limits for both the state and school districts. We conclude with a variety of short‑ and long‑term policy options-both of which we think the Legislature will need to take-in response to the issue.
How the Limit Works for the State
The SAL calculation has three steps: ( 1) c alculate the spending limit, ( 2) d etermine appropriations subject to the limit, and ( 3) d etermine the room (if any). These steps are described in this section and summarized in Figure 1 . DOF has the responsibility for executing these calculations. While the Legislature determines annual appropriations and defines key parameters of the calculation in statute, it does not have a direct role in administering the limit.
Calculate the Spending Limit
First, the state calculates the limit. This limit, as shown in the top part of Figure 1, is the previous year's limit grown for the SAL growth factor.
Build Off of 1978‑79 Base Year. The provisions of Proposition 4 keep real per capita government spending under the 1978‑ 79 l evel, adjusted for population. As such, today's limit is based on the total level of state spending, adjusted for a variety of factors, in 1978‑79 (known as the base year). In determining the base year, the Legislature had to make a variety of choices about how to count various appropriations. For example, the Legislature had to determine which types of spending would count at the state level versus the local level.
Increase Limit by Growth Factor. Each year, the state grows the limit by multiplying the previous year's limit by a growth factor. The two most important inputs to the growth factor are:
Measure of Economic Growth. This growth factor is calculated by taking: ( 1) C alifornia fourth quarter personal income, as measured by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, divided by ( 2) t he civilian population of the state, as measured by DOF. (The State Constitution refers to this measure as the "cost‑of‑living" adjustment.)
Measure of Population Growth. The SAL growth factor's second major input is change in population. To measure population, the formula uses a weighted average of the change in the school population and the change in the state's civilian population.
Determine Appropriations Subject to the Limit
Second, the state determines appropriations subject to the limit. These are determined by first estimating proceeds of taxes from all state sources and then subtracting exclusions.
Determine Proceeds of Taxes. All state proceeds of taxes are included in the limit regardless of their fund source. This means the limit applies not only to the General Fund but also all special funds that receive revenues from taxes. Revenues from nontax sources-like user fees-are not included in the SAL. Some revenues, such as taxes on cigarettes from Proposition 56 (2016), were excluded from the SAL by the voters. Federal funding also is excluded from the SAL. So, the first step in calculating appropriations subject to the limit is to estimate the total proceeds of taxes subject to the limit.
Assume All Revenues Subject to the Limit Are Appropriated. Under the constitutional provisions of the SAL, all tax revenues are considered appropriated unless explicitly excluded. For example, reserve deposits are considered appropriations in the year the deposit is made. This means there is no such thing as "unappropriated" tax revenues.
Reduce Appropriations for Exclusions. The Constitution allows the state to reduce proceeds of taxes for certain exclusions. These exclusions are:
Subventions to Local Governments. The Constitution allows subventions to local governments to be counted against that local government's limit (instead of the state's limit). The term "subvention" was not defined in Proposition 4. The implementing legislation passed in 1980 e stablished the definition of subvention as: "only money received by a local agency from the state, the use of which is unrestricted by the statute providing the subvention."
Debt Service. The Constitution defines this exclusion as: "appropriations required to pay the cost of interest and redemption charges ... on indebtedness existing or legally authorized as of January 1, 1979, or on bonded indebtedness thereafter approved according to law by a vote of the electors..." In implementing legislation, the Legislature chose not to include some outstanding debt that existed in 1979-such as unfunded pension liabilities-as an exemption under this language.
Federal and Court Mandates. The Constitution created an exclusion for appropriations that are required to comply with mandates imposed by the courts or the federal government. To qualify as a mandate for SAL purposes, the federal or court requirement must result in an expenditure for additional services "without discretion" or "unavoidably make the provision of existing services more costly." In our office's view, the mandate must have been created after 1978‑ 79 t o qualify as an exclusion. Otherwise, the cost of that mandate would have been included in the base year's limit.
Qualified Capital Outlay Projects. The Constitution allows expenditures on capital outlay projects to be excluded from appropriations subject to the limit. Statute defines this as: "an appropriation for a fixed asset (including land and construction) with a useful life of 10 o r more years and a value which equals or exceeds one hundred thousand dollars ($100,000)."
Certain Emergency Spending. The Constitution also allows expenditures on emergencies to be excluded from appropriations subject to the limit. However, those expenditures must meet three specific conditions. The spending must be: ( 1) r elated to an emergency declaration by the Governor, ( 2) a pproved by two‑thirds vote, and ( 3) d edicated to an account for expenditures relating to that emergency.
Determine the Room
Third, the state compares the limit (calculated in step 1) t o appropriations subject to the limit (calculated in step 2) t o determine the difference. If appropriations subject to the limit are less than the limit, the state has room under the SAL. If appropriations subject to the limit exceed the limit (on net) over any two‑year period, there are excess revenues. The Constitution requires that these excess revenues either be:
Appropriated for purposes exempt from the SAL.
Split between additional school and community college district spending and taxpayer rebates.
How the Limits Work for Other Entities
Proposition 4 n ot only created an appropriations limit for the state, but also for most types of local government entities, including: counties, cities, special districts, and local educational agencies. This section describes how the appropriations limits work for these other entities.
School and Community College Districts
District SAL Calculations. State statutes detail the process by which districts administer their limits. (All school districts, county offices of education, and community college districts have local appropriation limits. Throughout this section we use the term "district" to refer to these entities.) The key steps are:
Determine Base‑Year Appropriations Subject to Limit. Like the state, districts calculated their appropriations subject to the limit for the base year of 1978‑79. This required districts to determine proceeds of taxes, including their local property tax collections and subventions they received from the state, in that year. Like the state, districts determined their appropriations subject to the limit, less exclusions such as debt service. As implemented by the Legislature, districts counted a share of state funding at the district level, with remaining state funds, including funds for categorical programs, counted at the state level.
Grow Appropriations Limit. Like the state, districts grow their prior‑year limits to establish their current‑year limits. Specifically, each district adjusts its prior‑year limit for ( 1) s tatewide growth in per capita personal income, and ( 2) c hanges to its student population. School districts measure their student population using average daily attendance, whereas community colleges use full‑time‑equivalent enrollment.
Determine Appropriations Subject to Limit. After a district establishes its limit, it follows several steps to determine how much of its revenue from proceeds of taxes to count toward its limit. For most districts, proceeds of taxes is the sum of their share of the local property tax, parcel taxes, interest on investments, and general purpose state funding (for example, the Local Control Funding Formula for school districts or the apportionment formula for community colleges). The funding districts receive through categorical programs counts toward the state's limit and is not part of the district calculation. Similar to the state, districts can exclude expenditures related to meeting federal mandates or court orders.
Funding That Cannot Be Counted Toward District Limits Is Counted at the State Level. In most cases, districts have greater proceeds of taxes than they are able to count toward their local limits. The portion of funding (whether from the state or property taxes) that cannot be counted toward district limits is counted using the state's limit. The state has two ways to allow districts to spend above their limits. Either the state transfers some of its own limit to districts or it absorbs some of the district's excess appropriations and counts those at the state level. Either mechanism allows the districts to spend above their limits and reduce the state's room. Currently, there is about $ 17 b illion in district revenues above their limits that is counted at the state level.
Some Districts Have Room Under Their Limits. Although most districts have proceeds of taxes in excess of their local limits, about 10 p ercent of districts are below their limits. We refer to this difference between the limit and appropriations subject to the limit as "room." This situation can occur if a district had a historically high appropriations limit, or if a district has been experiencing relatively slow growth in funding. Collectively, districts have $ 5 b illion in room.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)

Successive waves of federal cuts to California’s safety net are hitting our shores — and hospitals.
H.R. 1 (aka the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”), the spending plan written by House Republicans and signed into law last year by President Donald Trump, included the largest reductions in U.S. history to food assistance and health care programs. Its intentionally punitive and retaliatory cuts to California’s Medicaid program, Medi-Cal, are projected to cost the state billions of dollars per year and lead to more than a million Californians losing access to health care.
In the Bay Area, these cuts are becoming painful.
As our news organization documented this month, the number of uninsured people in emergency rooms at Santa Clara Valley Healthcare and Alameda Health System has spiked year over year.

Endorsement: Reject San Mateo Community College District’s $848 million Measure V (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-reject-san-mateo-community-college-districts-848-million-measure-v/)
Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
Those county-run systems expect to collectively lose more than a billion dollars annually. Notably, while our systems and residents are scrambling to survive, rural America is receiving a $50 billion lifeline from House Republicans and President Trump to protect their health care systems.
Proposition 40 was written to prop up this state’s safety net in the face of these devastating cuts.
However, this measure is the wrong solution to a real problem.
We advise California voters to reject short-sighted, self-sabotaging Proposition 40.
And we recommend they reject equally myopic Propositions 41 and 42 — countermeasures that would not only nullify the billionaires tax but senselessly shackle the state’s fiscal future.
Killing Golden Goose
Proposition 40 risks long-term pain for short-term gain. It’s the ballot equivalent of eating your seed corn.
Here’s how it would work:
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% levy on the net worth of billionaires who were residents of California on January 1. The tax would be due next year, but the state’s 250 or so billionaires could spread the payments out over five years.
Ninety percent of the revenues raised — estimated anywhere between $40 billion to $100 billion, depending on the expert — would fund health care services. The rest would go toward education and food assistance and administration.
What distinguishes this tax isn’t just that it’s targeting a very base of extremely high-net worth individuals but also that it applies retroactively and taxes wealth, not income.
Wealth taxes are unpopular with many economists, including liberal ones, for several reasons:
They can force the sale of productive assets (e.g. stock shares, patents, copyrights, farmland, etc). They’re difficult to administer because determining the value of some intangible assets, unlike income, is more art than a science. And most injuriously, they can encourage capital flight, especially when executed by a state acting alone.
To be sure, the capital hasn’t fled California yet, but the capitalists have been.
Founders of some of Silicon Valley’s largest companies, including Sergey Brin, Larry Page, Peter Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg and Travis Kalanick, have changed their residencies or announced plans to cut ties with the state in one way or another.
What makes Proposition 40 so dangerously self-destructive is California’s extraordinary dependence upon taxing high-income earners. Over the last two decades, the top 1% of earners have paid approximately 45% of the state’s income taxes.
For that reason, the state’s most respected, nonpartisan authority on policy, the Legislative Analyst’s Office, forecasts short-term benefits but long-term costs:
California will “probably collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax,” according to the LAO. But those gains would likely be temporary.
That’s because the LAO worries that “billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away.”
In fact, the LAO projects that billionaires leaving the state would reduce the state’s General Fund revenues by “less than a billion per year.”
But the union that pushed this proposition — Services Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West — wants to gamble.
Its leaders created this to help themselves first and foremost, even at the expense of their typical allies. Opposition to this proposition includes the California Teachers Association, the Association of California School Administrators and the California Professional Firefighters, among several other public and private sector unions. These unions know they’ll suffer when the state’s General Fund takes a hit.
Even the liberal governor of this state is fiercely opposed.
“We can’t let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state’s tax code on its own terms,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom.
We couldn’t agree more.
Self-shackling
To counter Proposition 40, Building a Better California — a political action committee formed earlier this year and backed by Silicon Valley billionaires including Sergey Brin, Vinod Khosla and Eric Scmidt — created two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42.
If either Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax won’t take effect.
The problem is that these two propositions would do far more than nullify the billionaires tax. They would tie the hands of the state far into the future in ways we cannot abide.
Proposition 41
This initiative’s requirement for more audits could be valuable. It would mandate that the State Auditor scrutinize special taxes before they appear on the ballot as well as ongoing programs funded by special taxes. The LAO sees possible savings if the auditor’s recommendations are followed.
However, the problem with Proposition 41 is its second provision. It would prevent any new special taxes from being excluded from the “Gann Limit” — a strict state spending cap enacted in 1979. That means that voters could approve a new tax to address a pressing public need, only to discover that the state cannot spend the money it collects without being constrained by a constitutional limit written half a century ago.
California has changed radically since the 1970s. And its fiscal rules must leave the state with the flexibility to address issues voters of the era never had to deal with — six-figure college costs, seven-figure mortgages and 13-figure wildfire costs.
